parts.title: Boundaries
parts.intro: Punctuation: where sentences, clauses and phrases begin and end.

parts.title: Transitions
parts.intro: College Board files these under Expression of Ideas, not Standard English Conventions. They are here because the same first look applies: read the choices, then name the link. In every one the choices are transition words: decide how the second statement relates to the first before you read them.

concepts.title: End of sentence
concepts.spot: Choices set a period and capital letter against a comma or nothing, or show the same words in question order and in statement order.

items: A reported question after whether or if. The team asked whether the method would work at scale.
An exclamation mark as the right answer. The bank offers one once, as a wrong choice (9091458d).
A sentence that ends inside quotation marks. The period goes inside the closing mark: The label read “Do not open.”

concepts.title: Semicolon
concepts.spot: A semicolon is offered. If a transition word moves from one side of it to the other, ask which clause the transition belongs to.

items: ; however, with the transition opening the second clause. The first trial failed; however, the second succeeded. Here however belongs to the second clause, so the semicolon comes before it. In the bank however and though always belong to the clause they end (, however;), and 2.2 shows the other order only with even so, rather, for example and in that era. Ask which statement the word belongs to.
The 2.2 pattern with other transitions. The sample was contaminated; therefore, the result was set aside. Moreover, instead, nevertheless and as a result work the same way.

concepts.title: Colon
concepts.spot: A colon is offered. Check that the words before it form a complete sentence.

items: A colon before a quotation. The report ends with a warning: “No coast is safe.”
A colon wrongly placed after such as or including. Wrong: The exhibit holds tools such as: chisels, awls and saws. In the bank the wrong colons follow a verb (7.2) or a preposition (7.3).

concepts.title: Dash
concepts.spot: A dash is offered. Look for a second dash elsewhere in the sentence.

items: A single dash before a full clause that explains. The result was clear—the coating had failed. In the bank the single dash (4.2) is followed by a noun phrase, and when a colon and a dash are both offered the colon is never right.

A pair of dashes around a full clause. The comet—it returns every 76 years—was last seen in 1986. The bank prints one in two passages (908a76b8, 99dedf36), but in the twelve questions of 4.1 the words between the dashes never form a complete sentence.

concepts.title: Parentheses
concepts.spot: An opening parenthesis sits earlier in the sentence.

items: The right answer is the opening parenthesis, with the closing one printed. The asteroid (first seen in 1998) passed within the Moon’s orbit. The bank offers an opening parenthesis only as a wrong choice.
A whole sentence in parentheses. Its period goes inside: (The second trial gave the same result.)

concepts.title: Comma
concepts.spot: The choices set a comma against other marks or none, or add and or but. Nothing in the choices says that a comma is the answer, so find what stands on each side of the blank: the eight situations at the start of Part A.

items: Comma + so, yet, or, nor or for between two complete clauses. The samples had thawed, so the team started again. Right answers in the bank use only and and but; so is offered once, with no comma, as a wrong choice (267a13e2).
A describing who clause between commas. Franklin, who produced the image, was not named in the paper. The bank tests this only with which (6.6).
A comma between two adjectives that each describe the noun. a long, narrow bridge. Pairs like this are printed in passages but are never the blank.
A comma after a verb of saying, before a quotation. The inspector wrote, “The bridge is sound.”

concepts.title: No punctuation
concepts.spot: One choice has no mark at all. Ask what the words on either side of the blank are to each other.

items: Two verbs that share one subject. The team collected the samples and tested them the same day. No comma before and, because no second subject follows. No question in the bank turns on this.
Before because, if, when or unless, when the clause finishes the thought. The trial stopped because the funding ran out. The bank has this once, with whenever (cdbbbf94).
A describing clause the sentence needs, with who. The engineer who designed the valve was never credited. The bank tests this with that (7.5).
Between such as or including and what follows. Wrong: metals such as, copper and zinc.
A quotation worked into the sentence with that. The inspector wrote that “the bridge is sound.”

concepts.title: Subject–verb agreement
concepts.spot: One choice is singular and the others are plural, or the reverse.

items: Neither … nor and either … or: the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Neither the director nor the actors were told.
There is and there are: the subject follows the verb. There are several reasons for the delay. The bank’s one inverted question (8.10) starts with Among.
The number of is singular; a number of is plural. The number of entries has doubled. A number of entries have errors.
A group noun. The committee meets on Fridays. Team, staff and audience work the same way.
One of the + plural + who or that: the verb after who is plural. She is one of the scientists who study deep-sea vents.
The words along with, as well as and together with. The mayor, along with two aides, was present. The bank has in conjunction with (8.3).
Everyone, each, either or neither alone as the subject. Each of the samples was tested twice. The bank has each one of and every + noun.

concepts.title: Verb form: tensed or not
concepts.spot: One verb appears as a tensed form, an -ing form, a to form, or an -ed form.

items: The plain form after insist, suggest, propose or require that. The board required that each member sign the form. This form is printed in two passages (4bed4658, ecba68b5) but is never the blank.

The plain form after help, let or make. The coating helps the metal resist rust. The bank prints it once: in ee4aa2aa the answer is help and the words after the blank are it survive. The question itself is about agreement.
An -ing form after a preposition. The valve works by releasing pressure slowly.
Matching forms in a list. The plan was to map the site, to date the layers and to publish the results. A list of to forms is printed in da53d726.

Paired words: not only … but also, both … and, either … or. The same form follows each half: The method not only saves time but also reduces waste. The pair is printed in c9a677e9 but is not what that question asks.
Having + -ed opening the sentence. Having finished the survey, the team returned to camp. In the bank having is right once, in the middle of a sentence (9127635a).

concepts.title: Verb tense
concepts.spot: All four choices are tensed forms of one verb, in different tenses.

items: Will have + -ed with by + a future date. By 2050 the glacier will have retreated two kilometers. Offered 4 times in the bank’s tense questions, never right.
Has / have + -ed with for, over the past decade, recently or so far. The species has declined over the past decade. Both right answers in the bank follow since.
If … were, … would: an imagined present. If the ice were thicker, the lake would hold a vehicle.
Would have + -ed: an imagined past result. Without the grant the dig would have closed. Offered once in the bank, wrong.
Would + verb: the future seen from the past. In 1961 the agency promised that it would land a crew within the decade. Offered 2 times in the bank’s tense questions, never right.
Had + -ed with before or after. After the dam had failed, the valley flooded.
Who for people against which and that for things; whom as an object; whose against who’s. No pronoun question in the bank offers any of these.
A noun as the right answer because any pronoun would be unclear. When Lee met Ortiz, the engineer explained the fault. In the bank every right answer in concept 11 is a pronoun.
Those against that in a comparison. The wings of a bat are longer than those of a mouse. The bank prints that of in 13.3 but never tests it.
It’s or they’re as the right answer. It’s the first map to show the coast. Offered 15 times in the bank, never right.
Their against there; your against you’re. There is offered once (d4f173ec) and you once (166efaa2), both wrong. Your and you’re never are.

concepts.title: Plural and possessive nouns
concepts.spot: The same nouns appear with and without apostrophes.

items: Irregular plurals that own something. the children’s books, the women’s team. The bank has people’s once.
A name that ends in s. The bank’s passages write Adams’s, Harris’s and James’s. None is the blank.
One thing owned jointly by two owners. Watson and Crick’s paper. The bank’s two-owner question (12.4) is the opposite case, each owner with its own.
A time or an amount that owns. two weeks’ notice, a day’s work.

concepts.title: Modifier placement
concepts.spot: The sentence opens with a describing phrase and a comma; the choices reorder the words that follow.

items: Unlike X, and Like X, openers. Unlike its predecessors, the new telescope works in infrared. The subject must be the same kind of thing as X. The bank prints Like openers in two passages (3a35ddd1, 94de423a) and tests the idea only with Compared to that of and Compared with that of (13.3).
As a + noun. As a child, Ochoa built radios. The person who was the child must come next.
A describing phrase at the end of the sentence. It attaches to the nearest noun. Wrong: The team studied a fossil in the lab that was 40 million years old. The lab is not that old; the fossil is.

The blank is the opening phrase and the subject is printed. Choose the phrase that the printed subject can do or be. In all 26 modifier questions of the bank it is the other way round: the opener is printed and the blank begins with the subject.
Contrast words the bank never offers. despite this, in spite of this, at the same time, then again, yet, be that as it may. They do the work of nevertheless (14.3) or that said (14.4).
In fact correcting a mistaken idea. Many assume the fee is per car. In fact, it is per person. In the bank in fact always strengthens (16.3) and actually does the correcting.
Though at the very end of a sentence. The method is slow. It is reliable, though.
Result words the bank never offers. as a consequence, because of this, thereby, so, in that case, if so.
A word that gives the reason, not the result. After all points back to a cause: The team was not surprised. After all, the first trial had failed the same way. The bank never offers it.
Elaboration words the bank never offers. to illustrate, namely, in essence, put another way, to be precise, more precisely, that is to say.
A summing-up word as the right answer. In short or in sum after several sentences of detail. The bank offers such words 18 times and never makes one right.
Addition words the bank never offers. also, too, equally, in the same way, by the same token, along the same lines, further.
Time words the bank never offers. at first, initially, originally, in the meantime, simultaneously, since then, thereafter, until then, by then, at last.

Comment words the bank never offers. surprisingly, unsurprisingly, predictably, ironically, remarkably, notably, naturally, understandably. They work like fittingly (19.2): the writer’s view of how the second fact sits with the first.
Words of place and scope. here, nearby, in general, typically, in theory, in practice.

u1-5.rule: A Because… clause followed by a comma and a main clause belongs to that main clause. It cannot also hang off the sentence before it.

u1-6.rule: A transition such as however or for one can end a sentence. If it comments on the first statement it stays with that statement, and the period follows it.

u1-7.rule: A direct question puts the helping verb before the subject and ends with a question mark.

u1-8.title: Indirect question or plain statement: subject before verb, period
u1-8.rule: A question reported inside a statement (investigated how…, deciding which…) keeps statement order, subject then verb, and ends with a period.

u2-1.rule: A semicolon joins two main clauses with no conjunction. Each side must be able to stand alone as a sentence.

u2-2.rule: If the transition or opening phrase tells how the second clause relates to the first (an example of it, a correction of it, the time it applies to), it opens the second clause: semicolon before, comma after.

u2-4.rule: When the items in a series contain commas of their own, semicolons separate the items. Every boundary between items takes a semicolon.

u6-1.title: Comma + coordinating conjunction joining two main clauses
u6-1.rule: Two main clauses can be joined by a comma followed by and, but, or, so, yet, for or nor. The comma goes before the conjunction, never after it. In the bank the conjunction is always and or but.

first.intro: Read the four choices before the sentence. What changes from one choice to the next tells you which rule is being tested, and so what to look for when you read. Every question in this guide fits one of eight patterns.

pats.pat: The same words in all four. Only the marks differ.
pats.what: Always punctuation (Part A): no verb, pronoun or transition question has choices like this.
pats.check: What stands on each side of the blank: a complete sentence, a phrase, or two halves of one unit? Then use the table at the start of Part A.

pats.pat: The same words in two orders, ending in a question mark or a period.
pats.what: A question, or a statement about a question (rules 1.7 and 1.8).
pats.check: Is the sentence itself asking? Verb first takes a question mark. Subject first takes a period.

pats.pat: The marks change, and some choices add a word: and, but, that, which, while, or a transition.
pats.what: Punctuation with a clause boundary (Part A). 49 of the 70 add and, but or so; 13 add that, which or while; the other 8 add some other word.
pats.check: Count the complete clauses on each side. A choice that adds and or but with no comma before it has never been right.

pats.what: Agreement, verb form or tense (lessons 8 to 10). The three rows below split it.

sub.pat: One choice is singular and the others plural, or the reverse.
sub.what: 54 of these 55 test subject–verb agreement; 1 tests verb form.
sub.check: Find the subject and match its number. The one choice whose number differs from the other three was right in all 54 agreement questions; first check that the subject has no other verb.

sub.pat: Tensed verbs mixed with -ing, to or having forms.
sub.what: 48 of these 49 test verb form; 1 is a tense question with one to form as a decoy.
sub.check: Does the clause already have a tensed verb? If it does, the blank is not one.

sub.pat: Four tensed verbs with no number split.
sub.what: 30 of these 32 test tense. The other two set a bare -ed form against the same word with a helping verb (characterized / is characterized, highly prized / were highly prized): rules 9.9 and 9.10.
sub.check: Find the time word in the sentence or the one before it.

pats.pat: Pronouns: it, they, them, this, these, its, their.
pats.what: Pronouns (lesson 11). In 6 of them each choice is a pronoun with its verb (one uses / we use / they use / it uses); the pronoun is still what is tested.
pats.check: Find the noun the pronoun stands for. It can come after the blank.

pats.pat: The same nouns with and without apostrophes.
pats.check: For each noun ask two things: one or many, and does it own the next noun?

pats.pat: Four long choices that begin with different nouns.
pats.what: Modifier placement (lesson 13). Every choice has at least 6 words in all but one question.
pats.check: Decide what the opening phrase describes. That noun must come first.
Cover the choices and name the link between the two statements yourself. Then find the word that says it.

steps: Look at the choices and name the pattern.
Read the whole sentence that holds the blank, to its end. Run the one check for that pattern.
Read the sentence once more with your answer in place.
first.fine: The patterns and their counts are measured on the bank. The three steps are a suggested way to use them; they were not timed on anyone.

gives.intro: These are regularities in how the bank builds its answer choices: how often each pattern occurs and how often it held. A pattern that held every time here can still fail on a test, so each comes with the check that makes it safe. The exceptions are named, because they show what the check is for.

finds.title: One choice differs in number from the others
finds.count: 54 of 54 agreement questions: the odd one is the answer (Easy 19, Medium 16, Hard 19).
finds.note: It has to be so when agreement is the only thing tested. In 50 of the 54 all three wrong choices have the wrong number, and their tenses vary only to hide that: has / have + -ed is among the wrong choices in 48 questions and is / are -ing in 29. In the other 4 one wrong choice is an -ing form, which has no number and fails because the clause needs a tensed verb. The same split appears once outside agreement, and there it misleads. In 505054e3 the choices are dates / date / dating / has dated, the subject gets its verb later (remains), and the answer is dating. Check that the blank is the only verb its subject has.

finds.title: One tensed verb among -ing, to and having forms
finds.count: 22 of 23: the tensed verb is the answer.
finds.note: The miss is 512f0ac9: to forge / forging / forged / and forging. The sentence already has two verbs joined by and (re-created and then reprogrammed), so a third tensed verb cannot follow without another and. The answer is to forge.

finds.title: One -ing, to or having form among three tensed verbs
finds.count: 18 of 20 verb-form questions: the untensed form is the answer.
finds.note: Misses: 4bed4658 (would increase … and ____: the plain form create, because the helper would is shared) and 6d247c13 (____ by businessman: Created). The same shape turns up in 5 questions outside verb form, and the untensed form is wrong in all 5. 4 are agreement questions, where the number split comes first. The fifth is a tense question, cf08e2fd: will become / became / is becoming / to become. There the three tensed forms differ in time, which makes it a tense question, and to + verb is only a decoy.

finds.title: The three rules in that order
finds.count: They give an answer in 98 of the 136 verb questions, and the right answer in 93.
finds.note: The 5 wrong answers are the misses named in the three entries above. The other 38 questions need the full check: 30 tense questions, where you look for the time word, and 8 verb-form questions, where you look for the clause’s verb.

finds.title: A verb with a helping word: has kept, is keeping, had kept, will keep
finds.count: Offered 197 times across the 136 verb questions, right 16. A one-word tensed form (keeps, keep, kept, is, was) is offered 239 times and right 96.
finds.note: Is / are -ing is offered 45 times and never right. Has / have + -ed is offered 70 times and right 7. A will form is offered 31 times and right 2. Of the 16 right ones, 9 are tense questions where the sentence gives the reason (since, by + a past time, an earlier event, an if … had clause, a pointer to later, when + a past event); 3 are agreement questions, where it is the only choice with the right number; and 4 are verb-form questions, where it is the only tensed choice. So the wrong choices are mostly the longer tenses. Start from the one-word form and move to a longer one only when the sentence gives you the reason. The table at the start of Part B lists every form.

finds.title: Tense: the only choice in its time frame
finds.count: 25 of 31: the right answer is the only past form, the only present form or the only future form among the four.
finds.note: In the other 6 two or three choices share the time frame, and a finer point decides. Simple past, had + -ed and was -ing compete in 1f8cd95f (simple past is right) and d46ac7e7 (had + -ed is right). Simple present and are -ing compete in 96c720af and 96e5da01 (simple present is right in both). Has / have + -ed and simple present compete in 2d6f8304 and 35360da9 (has / have + -ed is right in both, after since). Two forms are close to pure decoys in tense questions: is / are -ing is offered 11 times and never right, and a will form is offered 27 times and right once.

finds.title: Simple past against has / have + -ed
finds.count: 4 of the 10 simple-past questions offer a has / have form as a rival: has / have + -ed in 3, has been -ing in 1.
finds.note: A finished date or period rules it out (from 1440 to 1473, In 1613, On March 27, 2004). Has / have + -ed is right only in the two questions with since.

finds.title: A common shortcut: by, as or to after the blank means the -ed form
finds.count: Holds in 5 of 9.
finds.note: By follows the blank in 5 questions. The -ed form is right in the 3 where by names the doer (by businessman, by the use of, by collectors) and wrong in the other two (survives by producing, goes by two names). As: two questions, both served, which is there as the sentence’s past-tense verb. To + a noun: two questions (attest to the value, have contributed to the project), neither a bare -ed form. The part worth keeping: an -ed word directly before by + the doer describes a noun and takes no helping verb.

finds.title: A choice with no punctuation at all
finds.count: Offered in 147 questions, right in 45.
finds.note: All 45 are the questions where the two sides of the blank belong together (concept 7). In the other 102 questions where a no-mark choice is offered, it is never right.

finds.title: A choice that adds and or but with no comma in front of it
finds.count: 46 choices, never right.

finds.title: and or but offered beside a period, a semicolon or a colon
finds.count: 28 questions: the choice with the conjunction is wrong in all 28.
finds.note: When no period, semicolon or colon is offered (20 questions), comma + and / but is right in 14. In the other 6 the words before the blank are not a complete clause (an opening Because or While clause or phrase, an aside, a noun waiting for its that clause), and the answer is a comma alone or no mark.

finds.title: however or though inside the choices
finds.count: 14 questions, all Hard. A comma comes before the word in all 14.
finds.note: After the word comes a semicolon in 9, a colon in 2, and a comma in 3: the three where one side is only a phrase. A semicolon or period placed before the word (; however, or . However,) is offered in all 14 and right in none. That is a fact about these questions, where the word always belongs with the words before it. Standard English also allows ; however, when the word opens the second statement: see “Could still appear” under Semicolon.

finds.title: A comma directly before that
finds.count: 5 choices, never right.
finds.note: That appears in 9 right choices, never with a comma before it.

finds.title: A colon among the choices
finds.count: 77 questions, right in 19.
finds.note: Right after a complete sentence that is followed by a list or by the thing it promised (10 of 10), or by a second complete clause that explains the first (9 of 12). Offered and wrong every time elsewhere: between words that belong together (27), beside an aside (16), inside a series (7), after an opener (3), before a trailing phrase (2). When a colon and a dash are both offered (25 questions) the colon is never right; the dash is right in 8.

finds.title: A dash among the choices
finds.count: 43 questions, right in 13.
finds.note: With another dash printed in the same sentence: right in 11 of 16. With none: right in 2 of 27 (2b512e65, where both dashes are inside the choice, and 92f309b2, a single dash before a closing detail). In the 5 where a dash is printed and the dash choice is still wrong, the printed dash either has its partner already (fa36d803, fdb16e20) or stands alone to introduce something (e41018de, f45ae404, b5ff8f8e).

finds.title: Semicolon and colon by difficulty
finds.count: Semicolon right: Easy 0 of 18, Medium 8 of 24, Hard 25 of 49. Colon right: Easy 0 of 23, Medium 2 of 18, Hard 17 of 36.
finds.note: On the bank’s Easy questions a semicolon or a colon is never the answer. You cannot see a question’s difficulty on the test, so treat this as background: these two marks are mostly the answers to hard questions and decoys elsewhere.

finds.title: A period and a semicolon both offered
finds.count: 37 questions. Neither is right in 30.
finds.note: The semicolon is right in 4: three are series semicolons (e2f77ae7, 05a14e18, c49e946e) and one is , however; set against . However, (b771d175). The period is right in 3 (73a6603c, 952fd392, 3a2d77d7). Only in 952fd392 do a bare period and a bare semicolon compete at the same spot, and there the second sentence already uses semicolons for a series. The bank never asks you to prefer one to the other on style.

finds.title: What College Board calls the wrong choices
finds.count: Of 639 wrong punctuation choices, its explanations say comma splice for 91, run-on for 82 and fragment for 34.
finds.note: A comma splice is two complete clauses joined by a comma alone. A run-on is the same with nothing between them. A fragment is a period in front of words that cannot stand alone. The other wrong choices get no single name: a mark between words that belong together, two different marks around an aside, a question mark on a statement.

finds.title: One singular pronoun among plurals, or the reverse
finds.count: 11 of 12: the odd one is the answer. The split occurs in 12 of the 26 pronoun questions.
finds.note: The miss is 42cc9236: this / that / these / it. The lone plural is wrong, and the choice is among three singulars.

finds.title: it’s and they’re
finds.count: Offered in 8 and 7 questions, right in none. There is offered once, wrong.
finds.note: The 6 its / it’s / their / they’re questions (11.7) come out its 3, their 3. 5 of the 6 are Hard. The difficulty is finding the owner, which stands after the blank in 2 of them.

finds.title: An apostrophe directly before a verb, a preposition or closing punctuation
finds.count: Removes 28 of the 60 wrong choices in the 20 apostrophe questions and never the right one. It settles 4 questions outright.
finds.note: Widened to anything that cannot be owned (an adverb, who or that, but), it removes 33. It does nothing in 8 questions, where every apostrophe sits before a noun and the question is whether there is one owner or several. And is the exception to the widened rule: rock’s and rap’s is right.

finds.title: Modifier questions: the first noun of each choice
finds.count: Exactly one choice begins with the thing the opening phrase describes in 26 of 26.
finds.note: No second test is ever needed. Choices that begin it is, it was or there are: 6, all wrong. Choices that begin with a when clause: 3, all wrong. Two right answers are passive (684b8bd2, a14eef71), so passive voice is not a flaw to look for.

finds.title: A choice that begins with a possessive (X’s Y)
finds.count: 14 choices, right in 4.
finds.note: Some prep guides call this a trap. It is one when the opener is an action that needs its doer (Knowing …, By reducing …, Upon recovering …): wrong in 7 of 7. When the opener describes a thing, X’s Y can be exactly that thing: right in 4 of 7 (Julian’s 1935 synthesis, silica glass’s atomic arrangement, Iceland’s parliament, Chraïbi’s debut novel).

finds.title: The longest choice in a Part B question
finds.count: Right in 10 of the 153 Part B questions that have one longest choice. In agreement and tense questions: 0 of 55.
finds.note: The shortest choice is right in 84 of the 173 that have one shortest choice. This fits how the wrong choices are built: by adding helping verbs (has been, are … -ing), wordy openings (it was … who, there are … who) or extra apostrophes. It is a tendency and not a rule: the longest choice is right in 4 verb-form questions, 4 pronoun questions, 1 apostrophe question and 1 modifier question. Length is counted in characters.

finds.title: The answer letter
finds.count: In the whole bank of 1,845 questions A, B, C and D are right 462, 457, 434 and 492 times. In the 615 in this guide: 141, 144, 146 and 184.
finds.note: D is a little ahead in this guide (30%), but over the whole bank the four letters stay within a few points of one another (27% for D). There is nothing here to use.

finds.title: How many transitions the bank uses
finds.count: 109 different words and phrases are offered. 71 are right at least once. 38 never are.
finds.note: The table at the start of Part C lists all of them.

finds.title: Words that sum up: in conclusion, in sum, in summary, to conclude, in the end
finds.count: Offered 18 times, never right.
finds.note: Other near-pure decoys: regardless (0 of 16), furthermore (0 of 8), in other words (1 of 36), similarly (3 of 36), nevertheless (3 of 35), for example (8 of 64).

finds.title: however or though already printed in the sentence before the blank’s sentence
finds.count: 9 questions. The blank is a result word in 8 and never another contrast word.
finds.note: The eight are as a result (3), therefore (2), hence (2) and in response (1). The ninth is 827afb27, where the sentence after However, not all conifer species are evergreen. gives an example. The contrast has been spent; the blank does another job.

finds.title: Two choices that do the same job
finds.count: Examples and details 13, additions 10, restatements 6, results 2: in all 31 questions with such a pair, both are wrong.
finds.note: A common tip says two choices from one category cancel. For those four categories they always do. For time words they never do (5 of 5): earlier and next, or then and lastly, mean different things, and one of them is the answer. For contrast words the pair contains the answer in 4 of 51, each time because the two do different jobs (instead beside regardless, of course beside however, by contrast beside granted). When both are plain “despite that” words (however, nevertheless, nonetheless, still, regardless, that said), both are wrong in 10 of 10.

finds.title: A contrast word among the wrong choices
finds.count: 116 of the 139 questions whose answer is not a contrast word offer at least one.
finds.note: Whenever the answer is a result, time, example, addition or emphasis word, contrast words are the most common wrong choice. The table “What the wrong choices do” at the start of Part C has the full count. So a contrast word among the choices tells you nothing by itself; test it by asking whether the second statement really goes against the first.

finds.title: Four choices, four different jobs
finds.count: 107 of 194 questions draw their four choices from four different categories; 82 from three; 5 from two.
finds.note: So in more than half the questions, naming the link between the two statements leaves exactly one choice.

finds.title: Where the blank sits
finds.count: First word of its sentence in 161 of 194. Inside the sentence in 33.
finds.note: Inside means after the subject (13), after a semicolon (10), after an opening phrase (6), after the verb (2), after a dash (1) or between two examples (1). After an opening phrase the answer is a contrast word in 6 of 6. After the subject it is a contrast word in 7, an example word in 4 and a result word in 2. Blanks inside the sentence make up 9% of Easy questions, 19% of Medium and 29% of Hard.

finds.title: though and later as answers
finds.count: Though: 4 of 4 sit inside the sentence between commas. Later: 3 of 3 are followed at once by in + a year or month.

intro: The bank rates 199 of the 615 questions Hard, 176 Medium and 240 Easy. The Hard ones are not spread evenly: the 21 rules below hold 118 of the 199.

By concept: Colon 17 of 19 Hard, Semicolon 25 of 33, Modifier placement 16 of 26. No Verb tense question is Hard (0 of 31); 2 of the 30 Time and order transitions and 2 of the 20 apostrophe questions are.

rows.why: The name looks like an aside, and the choices offer commas around it. They would be right only if the name could be lifted out.

rows.title: After a transition that closes the first clause (“, though;”)
rows.why: A transition sits at the boundary, and every choice moves the marks around it.

rows.title: Introducing a full clause that explains the first
rows.why: The second clause often opens with as, whereas or a phrase, so it reads like a continuation.

rows.title: Two sentences; the second opens with a participial phrase
rows.why: The second sentence opens with an -ed or -ing phrase that looks like the tail of the first.

rows.title: Separating items in a series whose items contain commas
rows.why: The semicolon separates items, not clauses. You see it only by reading on to ; and.

rows.title: A prepositional phrase and an aside are stacked between subject and verb
rows.why: Two things stand between the subject and its verb: an of phrase and an aside.

rows.title: Result or consequence
Joining two main clauses
rows.why: No linking word marks the join. You have to see two complete clauses.

rows.title: Introducing a noun phrase that names what was just promised
rows.why: A colon before a single noun phrase looks abrupt beside a semicolon or a period.

rows.title: One of a pair of dashes around an aside
rows.why: The other dash of the pair is printed some way from the blank.

rows.title: “Its” / “their” (possessive) versus “it’s” / “they’re” (contraction)
rows.why: The owner stands far from the blank or after it, with nouns of the other number in between.

rows.title: Two sentences; the second opens with a prepositional or adverbial phrase
rows.why: The phrase that opens the second sentence (According to …, With …) can be read as the end of the first.

An aside between commas or dashes sits between subject and verb
-ing phrase between commas, interrupting subject and verb
rows.why: The subject is followed by a comma and an -ing phrase. Its verb comes only after the second comma.

rows.title: -ing phrase with no commas; the main verb arrives later
rows.why: No commas mark off the -ing phrase, so the blank looks like the place for the verb. The verb comes later.

rows.title: Opening past-participle phrase
rows.why: All four choices say nearly the same thing. Only the noun that comes first differs.

rows.title: Opening preposition + -ing (“By reducing…”, “Upon recovering…”)
rows.why: All four choices say nearly the same thing. Only the noun that comes first differs.

hard.fine: Difficulty is the bank’s own rating of each question. “What makes it hard” is this guide’s reading of what those questions share; it is not measured.

structure.title: Find what stands on each side of the blank
structure.intro: Every punctuation question in the bank comes down to one of eight situations. Decide which one you are in, and the mark follows. A complete clause has its own subject and tensed verb and could be a sentence.

rows.head: Two complete clauses
rows.tell: Read past any opening phrase until you meet the second subject and its verb.

rows.head: A complete clause, then a list or the thing it promised
rows.tell: The words before the mark could end with a period. The words after could not stand alone.

rows.head: A complete clause, then a trailing phrase that describes
rows.tell: After a complete clause comes a piece that could not stand alone as a sentence: an -ing phrase, a noun phrase that renames or sums up, such as …, or a while (meaning whereas) clause.

rows.head: An aside inside the sentence, or a describing clause
rows.tell: Lift the words out and the sentence still works. The two marks must match.

rows.head: An opening clause or phrase, then the main clause
rows.tell: The sentence starts with Although, While, Because, an -ing or -ed phrase, or a noun phrase, and has not yet reached its subject.

rows.head: Items in a series
rows.tell: Semicolons when the items have commas inside them: look for ; and before the last item.

rows.head: Two halves of one unit
rows.tell: Subject and verb, verb and object, preposition and object, title and name, noun and its that clause.

rows.head: A question, or a statement about one
rows.tell: Verb before subject asks. Subject before verb reports.

structure.subtitle: Two complete clauses: which of the four marks
steps: If some choices add and or but and none offers a period, semicolon or colon, the answer is comma + and / but in 14 of 20. The other 6 are not two clauses at all.
If a period or a semicolon is offered, it is right when what follows could stand alone. The bank does not make you choose between the two.

A colon joins two clauses when the second explains or spells out the first. In 8 of the 9 such questions the other choices offer no period or semicolon, only commas, nothing, and or while, so the colon is the only mark on offer that can stand between two clauses.
If however or though sits at the boundary, put a comma before it and the strong mark after it (9 semicolons, 2 colons).

verbs.title: Verb questions: four situations
verbs.intro: 136 of the 208 questions in this part change one verb. Read the whole sentence that holds the blank, then decide which of four situations you are in. A tensed verb is one that can be the verb of a clause: kept, is, has collected.

rows.head: The clause already has its tensed verb, so the blank is not one
rows.tell: The subject’s tensed verb stands somewhere else in the clause. To + verb follows a verb that calls for it, or gives a purpose. An -ing form describes the noun before it or adds a result after a comma. An -ed form says what was done to the noun.

marks.label: -ed form, or no verb at all

rows.head: The clause has no tensed verb yet, so the blank is one
rows.tell: Read to the end of the sentence. A verb inside a who, that or which clause belongs to that clause and does not count for the main subject.

rows.head: The tensed choices differ in number
rows.tell: Find the subject by removing what stands between it and the verb: an of phrase, an aside between commas or dashes, an -ing phrase.

rows.head: The tensed choices differ in time
rows.tell: Look for a date, since, by + a time, currently or today, and at the tense of the verbs around the blank.

verbs.formsTitle: Every verb form the bank offers
verbs.formsIntro: The four choices of each of the 136 verb questions, sorted by form and written with one model verb, keep. After each form: how many times it is the right answer, of how many times it is offered.

forms.group: Forms that give the clause no tensed verb

verbs.formsNote: Kept stands for any -ed form: 3 of its 20 right answers are participles that describe a noun (9.9, 9.10), and the rest are simple past. Keep is the present with a plural subject, or the plain form after a shared helper.

rest.head: The choices change a pronoun
rest.tell: Find the noun it stands for and match its number. For its and their, find the owner; it can come after the blank.

rest.head: The choices move apostrophes
rest.tell: For each noun ask: one or many, and does it own the next noun? Cross out any apostrophe that stands before a verb or a preposition.

rest.head: Four long choices begin with different nouns
rest.tell: Decide what the opening phrase describes or who does it. The choice that begins with that noun is the answer.

glossary.def: A subject and a tensed verb that can stand alone as a sentence. Also called a complete clause here. Many grammar guides call it an independent clause.
A subject and a tensed verb opened by a word such as because, although, while, that, which or who. It cannot stand alone.
A group of words with no subject and tensed verb of its own.
A verb form that can be the verb of a clause: kept, is, has collected. Also called a finite verb.
An -ing form, a to form, or an -ed form with no helping verb: keeping, to keep, kept by. On its own it cannot be the verb of a clause. Also called non-finite.
Extra information set off by a pair of commas, dashes or parentheses. The sentence still works when it is lifted out. College Board calls it a supplement.
A clause or phrase that comes before the subject of the main clause.
Two main clauses joined by a comma alone.
Two main clauses with nothing between them.
Words punctuated as a sentence that contain no main clause.
The noun a pronoun stands for.
A word such as this, these, its or their placed in front of a noun.
And, but, or, so, yet, for, nor: the words that can join two main clauses after a comma.
A describing clause is essential when the sentence needs it to say which thing is meant; it takes no commas. It is nonessential when it only adds information; it goes between commas.
A noun phrase set beside another noun to rename it: Lagos, the country’s largest city.
A phrase built on an -ing or -ed form that describes a noun: hoping to win, known for its speed.
The -ed form that follows has or was, or that describes a noun on its own: built, written, prized.
To + the plain form of a verb: to keep.
A noun followed by an -ing or -ed form, attached to a sentence by a comma with no linking word: its engine still running.
Two verbs that share one subject, joined by and: mixed the paint and hung the canvas.

glossary.term: Present perfect, past perfect, past progressive
glossary.def: has kept; had kept; was keeping.
Itself, themselves: used when the doer and the receiver are the same.
One recognisable form of a rule: what sits around the blank and how the right answer looks.

absent.intro: None of the 421 Conventions questions is decided by any of the following, so there is no example to show. Other prep material may teach them.
items: Who against whom, and subject against object pronouns generally (I / me, he / him).
Who’s against whose, and your against you’re.
There against their: it appears once, as a wrong choice (question d4f173ec, filed under 12.5).
Its’ with the apostrophe after the s: never offered.
Agreement with neither … nor, either … or or everyone, or with the words along with or as well as. One question uses in conjunction with (ecba68b5).
A comma between two adjectives. A pair such as “random, continuous movement” appears in passage text but is never the blank.
Whether a comma or period goes inside or outside a closing quotation mark. The convention shows in the choices of two questions (fe41f258, 3ed5ebb4) but does not decide them.

method: The source is an export of College Board’s SAT Suite Question Bank: 1,845 Reading and Writing questions. This guide covers the 421 filed under Standard English Conventions (213 Boundaries, 208 Form, Structure, and Sense) and the 194 filed under Transitions.

Each of the 421 Conventions questions was read together with its official explanation and filed under exactly one rule. The concept and rule names in Parts A and B are this guide’s own: College Board sorts these questions only into Boundaries and Form, Structure, and Sense.
Each Transitions question is filed by the transition that is its correct answer, except one where the word does a different job in its passage (42e6cc83).

For the catalog’s second edition every question was read a second time and assigned to one version of its rule. The second reading was done by the same reader as the first; no independent person has checked the filing.

Where a version’s label names the answer words, the marks or a position that a script can test, every question of that version is tested against it: 67 of the 234 versions, holding 243 questions. The other versions rest on reading alone, and so do the notes under them; the notes were re-read against their questions once more before that edition was published.

One outside check was available. College Board’s explanation names the convention being tested in 177 of the 208 Form, Structure, and Sense questions, and that name matches this guide’s concept in 171. The other 6 are five agreement questions it labels “verb forms” while explaining them by number, and one it labels punctuation. Of the 107 Boundaries explanations that name a specific structure, 106 match the rule here.
Passages, fragments, answer choices and answer letters are copied from the bank by script and checked against its answer key. The rules and explanations are written for this guide.

Words quoted inside the explanations are checked against their question by script: the 266 quoted phrases in the worked examples (15 of them are glosses or shortened sentences and not the bank’s words, such as “it is” for it’s), the 41 quotations in the sections on the answer choices, and the 239 words and phrases that version labels and notes put in italics (14 of those are patterns with placeholders, such as In X, … in Y).

The counts in “Eight patterns in the answer choices” and “What the choices give away” are computed from the bank by script. The SAT Grammar Catalog asserted each one when its page was built; this site copies them unchanged.
Counts describe this bank. They are not a forecast of what one test will contain.
